title: Learning a Dispatch Policy
intro: A policy learns which decision reduces cost over the whole operating period.
content:
Every **120 seconds**: observe → choose a feasible action → receive reward.

$$G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}r_k$$

$$J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}[G_0]$$

**Project setting:** $\gamma=1$ · finite 240-minute episode.
takeaway: Dispatch may incur deadhead cost now and reduce waiting later. Learn from the full consequence.

title: Policy Gradient
intro: Learn action probabilities directly from the consequences of sampled decisions.
content:
The network produces a **logit** for each action; softmax gives its probability.

$$\pi_\theta(a\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_a(x))}{\sum_b\exp(z_b(x))}$$

$$\widehat g\propto\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid x_t)\,w_t$$

$x$: observation and available history. $w_t$: a fixed quality signal during the actor update.
takeaway: The gradient passes through the policy network. The simulator does not need to be differentiable.

title: REINFORCE and the Baseline
intro: Score a decision using the return observed from that step to the end of the episode.
content:
$$G_t=r_t+r_{t+1}+\cdots+r_{T-1}\qquad(\gamma=1)$$

Demand and traffic make raw returns noisy. Subtract a reference return for the same situation:

$$w_t=G_t-b(x_t)$$

The question becomes: **was this outcome better than expected?**
takeaway: REINFORCE is a conceptual foundation here, not an experimental controller. This baseline differs from Fixed / Proportional / Threshold.

title: Actor–Critic and Bootstrapping
intro: The actor chooses an action; the critic estimates the return still to come.
content:
Use the observed reward and the next value estimate instead of waiting for the whole episode.

$$y_t=r_t+\gamma(1-d_t)V_\phi(x_{t+1})$$

$$\delta_t=y_t-V_\phi(x_t)$$

$d_t=1$ at a true episode termination; otherwise $d_t=0$.
takeaway: A critic predicts from experience. It does not know future demand or traffic.

title: Advantage and GAE
intro: Advantage measures how much better or worse an outcome is than the critic expected.
content:
$$\delta_t=r_t+\gamma(1-d_t)V_{old}(x_{t+1})-V_{old}(x_t)$$

$$\widehat A_t=\delta_t+\gamma\lambda(1-d_t)\widehat A_{t+1}$$

$$\widehat G_t=\widehat A_t+V_{old}(x_t)$$

**Project:** $\gamma=1$, $\lambda=0.95$. Compute backwards through the rollout.
takeaway: True episode end: stop bootstrapping. Rollout ends mid-episode: bootstrap from the last observation.

title: From A2C to PPO
intro: Keep the actor–critic structure, but make repeated updates on one rollout more cautious.
content:
**A2C:** collect parallel experience → estimate advantage → update the shared policy.

$$L_{actor}=-\mathbb E[\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid x_t)\widehat A_t]$$

**PPO:** compare current and collection-time probabilities, then clip the actor objective.

This supports multiple minibatches and epochs on a recently collected rollout.
takeaway: A2C explains the progression to PPO. The study does not compare A2C against MaskablePPO.

title: PPO Ratio, Clipping and Loss
intro: Compare the same sampled action under the current policy and the policy that collected it.
content:
$$\rho_t(\theta)=\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid x_t)}{\pi_{old}(a_t\mid x_t)}$$

$$L^{clip}=\mathbb E\!\left[\min\!\left(\rho_t\widehat A_t,\operatorname{clip}(\rho_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\widehat A_t\right)\right]$$

**$\epsilon=0.2$:** ratio reference range **[0.8, 1.2]**.

Clipping limits the incentive in the objective; it does not enforce a hard ±20% probability bound.
takeaway: PPO clipping acts on the objective; gradient clipping limits gradient norm to 0.5. Learning rate: 0.0003.

title: Why MaskablePPO?
intro: The environment defines feasible actions; the policy learns which feasible action to choose.
content:
**221 logits** include state-dependent invalid actions. Apply the mask before sampling:

$$\pi_\theta^{mask}(a\mid x,m)=\frac{m(a)\exp(z_a(x))}{\sum_bm(b)\exp(z_b(x))}$$

An invalid action has probability **0**. Valid actions are renormalized; **NOOP** remains valid before terminal.

During updates, both probabilities use the sample’s original mask $m_t$.
takeaway: Store the mask with every sample. Use it for collection, optimization and evaluation; compute entropy over valid actions.

title: One Algorithm, Three Encoders
intro: All three configurations use MaskablePPO; they differ in how they represent the observation.
content:
**Trainer:** `MaskablePPO("MultiInputPolicy", ...)`

The actor and critic share **128 features**, then use separate heads. The action mask applies to the actor distribution.
takeaway: GRU10 resets its hidden state each forward; it is not recurrent across decisions. Belief20-fade is a local demand estimate, not a full POMDP belief.

title: Controlled Training Protocol
intro: Hold the algorithm, environment and training budget constant when comparing encoders.
content:
| Data and replication | Setting |
|---|---|
| Training / validation | 500 / 100 scenario days |
| Model seeds | 11 · 22 · 33 |
| Transitions / configuration / seed | 245,760 |
| Parallel environments / steps each | 4 / 256 |
| Minibatch / epochs | 256 / 4 |

**3 encoders × 3 seeds = 9 independent runs.**
takeaway: 500 scenario days do not mean one pass through the data. Transitions measure the training budget; validation does not update weights.

title: Collecting a Rollout
intro: A rollout is a batch of experience collected with fixed policy weights, not a single episode.
content:
$$N_{rollout}=4\times256=1024\text{ transitions}$$

**Episode:** 240 minutes = 120 decisions. A 256-step collection can cross episode boundaries.

Store **observation, action, reward, episode boundary, old value, old log probability and action mask**.
takeaway: Keep episode boundaries: do not carry rewards or advantages from one operating day into the next.

title: Updating from the Rollout
intro: Compute fixed targets, then reuse the fresh rollout for a limited number of optimizer steps.
content:
$$1024/256=4\text{ minibatches per epoch}$$

$$4\text{ minibatches}\times4\text{ epochs}=16\text{ optimizer steps}$$

**240 rollouts / run:** $245760/1024=240$.

Old log probabilities, old values and return targets stay fixed; current network outputs change after every update.
takeaway: This is on-policy learning with short-term rollout reuse. After the update, collect new experience with the updated policy.

title: Validation Measures Dispatch Quality
intro: Use held-out days to judge the controller; training loss alone does not measure dispatch quality.
content:
$$C_{val}=\frac{1}{N_{val}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{val}}C_{core}^{(i)}$$

Evaluate every **12,288 training transitions** on **100 validation days**.

**Training:** sample feasible actions to explore.

**Validation:** choose the highest-probability valid action; keep weights fixed.
takeaway: Train updates weights; validation selects checkpoints; test reports final performance. Core cost is a weighted service/operation objective, not money.

title: Select the Best Checkpoint
intro: Choose the lowest eligible validation cost, rather than automatically using the last policy.
content:
| Model / seed | Initial cost | Best cost | Selected step |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| MLP10 / 22 | 14,598.7 | 13,114.0 | 98,304 |
| GRU10 / 11 | 18,075.8 | 13,189.8 | 172,032 |
| Belief20-fade / 22 | 16,155.9 | 13,125.6 | 86,016 |

Actual validation records · **245,760 transitions** per run.
takeaway: Step 0 is reference only. On a tie, keep the earlier checkpoint. Save best.zip, last.zip, history and run metadata; use best.zip for test.

title: The Complete Training Workflow
intro: Alternate experience collection and policy updates, then evaluate the selected policy on test days.
content:
During collection, scheduled validation can save a new best checkpoint. After collection, compute GAE and update the policy.

Repeat until **245,760 transitions**, then save the final policy and metadata.

For test or inference, load **best.zip** and keep weights fixed while making a new dispatch decision every 120 seconds.
takeaway: The policy is trained. The next section asks whether it improves cost and service quality on held-out test conditions.
